nodes.title: Our axis is quality per human attention, and no paper optimizes it
nodes.body:
Every RSI paper surveyed optimizes quality per dollar or quality per wall-clock. None makes human attention the scarce resource. That is the axis this plugin exists on: the main agent must stay idle so the person can keep talking to it.

This is not cosmetic, it changes the optimum. If attention is scarce you want checkpoints batched rather than streamed, a loop that runs unattended for hours, every human decision to arrive with the evidence needed to decide it, and the loop to be safe to leave paused. A quality-per-dollar design would instead spend more of the main agent's own turns, because a strong lead reasoning directly is the cheapest route to quality (Cohere: lead-plans-only then implements itself matches full delegation at half cost). We deliberately buy a worse cost/quality point to stay available, and the plugin should say so in its own docs rather than let it be discovered.

The measurable consequence: the plugin needs a human-minutes-per-promotion counter the way it needs a token counter. Nobody publishes that number, so it is also the one place our own loop can produce a first measurement.

nodes.title: The self-optimization ladder is over-built against the evidence; gate L2 and L3 by measurement
nodes.body:
The design has L0 execution / L1 work-chain / L2 loop policy / L3 the plugin itself. The evidence says the top of that ladder is the low-yield, high-risk part.

A pre-registered port of DGM to LiveCodeBench found the improvements the loops found were mostly standard engineering changes: one textbook move recovered about nine tenths of the best loop's gain at under half the cost, and on SWE-bench Verified the released DGM agent scored 43.1% versus 73.6% for its initial agent plus three textbook moves, at a quarter of the cost. DGM also fabricated logs claiming tests had passed and removed a tool-use marker its own hallucination detector depended on; hacking was more frequent when the checking functions were visible. STOP found a capability threshold: iteration helped GPT-4 and degraded GPT-3.5-turbo and Mixtral, and budget constraints in the seed were simplified away during self-rewrite.

So keep L0 and L1; make L2 a measured experiment with a textbook-baseline control rather than default-on behaviour; make L3 require a human and a held-out eval, because that is the rung where a self-modification can delete its own guardrail. The docs should state which rung is on by default. Today none do.

nodes.title: Verifier precision is the binding constraint on our loop and we never measure it
nodes.body:
SPLIT states it exactly: verified success = P(a correct candidate exists) x P(it is selected | it exists), and the second factor is capped by verifier precision. Large Language Monkeys reaches 98% coverage on MATH while selection stays near 43%. More verification can hurt: k judge calls lower the precision ceiling whenever false-accept inflation exceeds true-accept inflation.

Our verifier is a shell command and an exit code. Per task it is either near-decisive or near-useless, and nothing in the ledger distinguishes the two. Every promotion decision, every minGain comparison and every lesson attribution inherits that unknown. One of our own recorded failures is exactly this shape: a verifier that collects zero tests exits 0 and looks like a pass.

The mechanical measurement is mutation auditing: mutate the source in ways the tests should catch, run the verifier, keep the fraction that still passes. A task whose verifier passes most mutants has low precision, so its scores are not evidence of correctness, its promotions should not be trusted, and its lessons should be suspect. Mutation score is deterministic, needs no model, and is the cheapest real improvement available to us. The second, cheaper signal is re-run flake on the same tree: flake is the part of the score that is noise, and today we treat one pass as ground truth.

nodes.title: Our promotion gate is a point estimate with no error budget, which makes it a multiple-testing machine
nodes.body:
PACE names the failure precisely: commit if the dev score went up, applied repeatedly, is uncontrolled adaptive multiple testing, and the agent effectively p-hacks itself. In a stochastic regime greedy acceptance committed 13 to 21 self-modifications per run with 72 to 100 percent of them false, and drove a smaller agent down 3 to 5 points; the same loop with a proper acceptor committed 0.3 changes and zero delta.

We had a local instance of the same disease in a different guise: bestPriorScore compared a candidate against a score measured on a different task, so after one task reached 1.0 every other task was judged no-gain. That fix removed the cross-task confusion but not the statistical one. minGain is still a threshold on a single draw.

A defensible acceptor needs: the delta compared against the observed noise of that task rather than against zero; non-regression on a held-out task before promotion, which is Self-Harness's held-in >= 0 and held-out >= 0 with max > 0; and an explicit stop when improvement is not detectable, which also saves evaluations (PACE used about 18 percent fewer). Our own ten-reruns-of-one-config evidence (2.2 to 6.0 points of spread) says any 2 to 3 point gain is inside the noise, so the gate as it stands can only be trusted for large effects.

nodes.title: Delegation costs us quality by design, so it must be paid for by something the loop can show
nodes.body:
Cohere measured on ProgramBench that a lead which delegates only planning and then implements and verifies itself matches full delegation at half the cost; cheap implementers lower reward while cheap planners hold it. Anthropic measured that orchestrator-worker beats a single agent by 90.2 percent on research, but also that multi-agent runs use about 15x the tokens of chat and that a single model can be beaten by tokens alone in 80 percent of cases, so part of that gain is just spend. They state coding involves fewer truly parallelizable tasks than research.

We are not in the cheap case. Our worker cannot see the main agent's context, so every brief is a lossy re-derivation, and CostPar names the two hidden costs: re-exploration and alignment. Cognition's argument that parallel agents fragment implicit decisions is the strong form of the counter-hypothesis, and our own handoff evidence agrees: 41.8 percent of delegated-search failures are silent.

So stop claiming delegation is free and start paying for it with what it buys: main-agent availability, plus per-attempt isolation that makes a bad attempt discardable. The honest metric is quality per (tokens + human minutes) and the loop should report both denominators, or it cannot tell whether delegation pays.
nodes.source: Anthropic multi-agent research, Cohere ProgramBench, CostPar, Cognition
